title: How the Titanic Worked: Part One
summary: Part one of a two-part Stuff You Should Know episode on the RMS Titanic. The hosts open by discussing the 1997 James Cameron movie and its accuracy and flaws, then cover the White Star Line's origins in a dinner-table decision to build bigger luxury liners to compete with Cunard, the design by Thomas Andrews and Alexander Montgomery Carlisle, the ship's size, rivets, engines, propellers, watertight compartments, coal consumption and a coal fire, the Harland and Wolff/Belfast construction and Great Gantry, and the ship's luxurious decks and class-divided accommodations from first to third class. They discuss the maiden voyage passengers and crew, notable people who missed the sailing (including Davy Blair's binocular key), ticket prices, the lifeboat shortage under the Board of Trade rules, untested lifeboat drills, and the near-collision with the SS New York at Southampton. The episode ends before the Titanic reaches open sea, with the ship leaving Queenstown on April 11.
topics: Titanic passengers who did not sail

segments.title: Opening banter and the 1997 Titanic movie
segments.summary: The hosts open the episode, note listener requests for a Titanic episode, and discuss James Cameron's movie: its accuracy, its romance and dialogue flaws, and the fact that the film cost about half as much as the ship in inflation-adjusted terms.

segments.title: Why the podcast delayed the Titanic topic and personal interest
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck explain they put off the Titanic for a long time because of the movie, and describe their interest in the wreck's underwater discovery and the research they did.

segments.title: The dinner that led to the Titanic and its sister ships
segments.summary: The hosts describe a dinner among White Star Line leaders J. Bruce Ismay and Lord William Pirrie, and their wives, where they decided to compete with Cunard's speed by building bigger, more luxurious ships rather than faster ones. The Titanic, Olympic and Britannic (originally named Gigantic) came out of this.

segments.title: Design, size and engineering of the Titanic
segments.summary: The designers, Alexander Montgomery Carlisle and then Thomas Andrews, planned the ship; the hosts describe its length, width and tonnage, the four funnels, the wrought iron rivets with excess slag, and the two huge reciprocating engines.

segments.title: Propellers, watertight compartments and the coal fire
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Titanic's three- and four-blade propellers, its sixteen watertight compartments with automatic doors that fed the unsinkable reputation, the coal consumption, and a coal fire that may have started before departure.

segments.title: Construction at Harland and Wolff and the Great Gantry
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Belfast dock and the Great Gantry used to build the ship, the roughly eleven thousand workers, the launch on May 31, 1911, and the completion and maiden voyage dates in 1912.

segments.title: Deck layout and class-based accommodations
segments.summary: The hosts walk through the ship's decks from the boat deck to the orlop deck, including the first-class promenade, Palm Court, the restaurants, the third-class poop deck, the Turkish bath, and the post office and workshops. They discuss the design's luxury across classes, including third-class cabins and washbasins, and the lack of bathtubs.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: A short break in the episode.

segments.title: Voyage route, passengers and people who missed the sailing
segments.summary: The ship's route from Belfast to Southampton, Cherbourg and Queenstown is covered. The hosts describe the passenger count, the people who sold or switched tickets or missed the boat including the Thomas Hart story, the wealthy industrialists who gave up their berths, and Davy Blair's missed post and crow's nest binocular key.

segments.title: Ticket prices and the size controversy
segments.summary: The hosts compare first-class fares (up to about $4,500 in 1912 money, roughly $66,000 to $120,000 today) to the average American wage and discuss third-class fares. They turn to the Board of Trade lifeboat requirements, the Merchant Shipping Act tonnage rule, and the undertested ship and untested lifeboat drills.

segments.title: Near collision with SS New York and departure
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Titanic's departure from Southampton, when suction from its propellers pulled the SS New York toward it, and the near miss averted by tug boats and the captain. The episode ends with the ship set to leave Queenstown on April 11 and a cliffhanger.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts tease part two and sign off.
